prompt: Three engineers are selected for a working group, all with the same role. Why does counting first, second and third picks overcount the groups?

options.text: The same engineer may occupy every role.
options.explanation: Members are distinct and are selected without replacement.

options.text: Every engineer must appear in every group.
options.explanation: A group is a subset of the available engineers.

options.text: Working groups cannot be represented by sets.
options.explanation: Their equal roles are exactly why a set is a suitable model.

options.text: Reordering the same three members creates several selection histories for one group.
options.explanation: The final group forgets the order of selection.

workedExample: Pick Alice, Ben and Cara. Choosing them in any order produces the same group. Every three-person group has the same number of such orders, so dividing out that uniform overcount gives combinations. Giving them distinct offices would instead make order matter.

prompt: For a list of distinct items, how do `itertools.combinations(xs, 2)` and `itertools.permutations(xs, 2)` differ?

options.text: Permutations include both orders of each pair; combinations include it once.
options.explanation: Distinct input positions produce two ordered versions of each unordered pair.

options.text: Combinations include both orders; permutations include it once.
options.explanation: This reverses the meaning of the two functions.

options.text: Permutations may reuse an input position twice.
options.explanation: Permutations select distinct positions; product with repetition would permit reuse.

options.text: Combinations contain only neighbouring input items.
options.explanation: They choose from any two positions, not only adjacent ones.

workedExample: Look at two distinct inputs, Alice and Ben. The permutations contain both Alice–Ben and Ben–Alice. The combinations contain one representative. Neither function repeats an input position within this pair; repeated values in an input list are a separate issue.

prompt: Which methods count three-person groups from ten distinct people exactly once? Select all that apply.

options.text: Choose the seven people left out.
options.explanation: Each excluded group has exactly one included complement.

options.text: Count ordered triples of distinct people, then divide by the number of orders of three distinct people.
options.explanation: Every group has the same number of ordered representations.

options.text: Allow repeated people in triples, then divide by that same number of orders.
options.explanation: Repeated entries are not valid three-person groups and do not have uniform multiplicity.

options.text: Fix one person and add groups containing them to groups excluding them.
options.explanation: These cases are disjoint and exhaustive.

options.text: Choose a pair and then a third person, without correcting duplicates.
options.explanation: Each final group can be produced by choosing any of its pairs first.

workedExample: Check whether each target group has one representation, or a known constant number that the method removes. Complement selection is bijective. Ordered triples have a constant overcount. Splitting on one person gives disjoint cases. Allowing repetitions changes the objects, while pair-then-third counts each group repeatedly.
